short: How much work an AI system handles in a given time, such as tokens generated per second or requests served per minute.
explain: Latency is how fast one customer is served; throughput is how many customers you can serve at once. Providers balance the two to control cost. For high-volume uses, like tagging thousands of clips or scoring every bet, throughput and cost per unit matter more than speed on any single request.
analogy: Latency is how fast one bet gets accepted; throughput is how many bets per second the platform can take on Super Bowl Sunday.

short: The small chunk of text a model reads and writes: often a whole word, sometimes part of one.
explain: Models don't see letters or whole words; they see tokens, each mapped to a number. As a rough rule, a token is about three-quarters of an English word, so a 1,000-word memo is roughly 1,300 tokens. Almost everything is measured in tokens: how much fits in the context window, how fast a model responds and what you pay.
analogy: Tokens are the chips at the table: the unit everything gets counted and priced in.

short: Charging for AI model use by the number of tokens processed, usually quoted as a price per million input and output tokens.
explain: Input tokens (what you send) usually cost less than output tokens (what the model writes), and bigger or reasoning models cost more. It's a form of usage-based pricing: you pay for what you consume rather than a flat fee. The price for a given level of capability has fallen dramatically year after year, yet total AI bills often rise because cheaper usage leads to far more usage.

short: An AI model's ability to use outside tools, like search, calculators, databases or other software, to get information or take action.
explain: On its own, a model can only produce text. Tool use lets it say, in effect, 'look up this player's stats' or 'run this calculation', have the software carry it out, and then use the result. It's the bridge between a model that talks and an agent that does.

short: Tensor processing unit: Google's custom AI chip, used to train and run its own models and rented to customers through Google Cloud.
explain: TPUs are an example of a big tech company designing its own silicon to reduce dependence on Nvidia and cut costs. Google's Gemini models are trained on them, and other AI labs have also signed deals to use them. They show that GPUs are not the only path to frontier AI.

short: The sportsbook function that manages prices and exposure: moving odds, setting limits and balancing liability as bets come in.
explain: Traders watch the flow of money, news and game state, and move lines or suspend markets to manage risk. AI and automation now handle much of the routine repricing and flag unusual activity, freeing human traders for judgment calls and big events. It's a natural home for agent-style monitoring tools, with humans kept in the loop on major decisions.

short: Building a model by feeding it vast amounts of data and adjusting its parameters until its outputs are good.
explain: Training a frontier model is enormously expensive, requiring huge clusters of GPUs running for weeks or months. It usually comes in stages: pre-training for broad knowledge, then post-training for behavior. Once training ends the model is frozen, and using it is called inference.
analogy: Training is the offseason and training camp; inference is game day.

short: The examples a model learns from, such as text, images, game logs or transactions; the biggest single influence on what a model can do.
explain: A model can only learn patterns that appear in its training data, including the gaps and biases. Frontier LLMs train on a large share of the public internet, books, code, licensed content and, increasingly, synthetic data generated by other AI models. Who owns, licenses and may legally use training data is now a major commercial and legal fight.
analogy: Training data is the film room: a scout who only watched one conference will misjudge players from all the others.

short: The neural network design, introduced in Google's 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need', that underpins nearly every modern LLM.
explain: Its key idea, called attention, lets the model weigh how every word in a passage relates to every other word at once; in 'the quarterback found the tight end because he was wide open', attention helps it work out that 'he' is the tight end. That design trains efficiently on GPUs and handles long context well, which is why it took over. The 'T' in GPT (generative pre-trained transformer, the name of OpenAI's model family) stands for Transformer.

short: A 1950 thought experiment by Alan Turing: if you can't tell a machine's conversation from a human's, should we call it intelligent?
explain: For decades it was the pop-culture finish line for AI. Modern chatbots can pass casual versions of it, which mostly showed that fluent conversation is not the same as reliable intelligence. Researchers now rely on harder, task-specific benchmarks instead.

short: The United States' approach to AI: mostly executive actions and sector rules at the federal level, plus a growing patchwork of state laws.
explain: There's no comprehensive federal AI law as of 2026; federal policy has shifted with each administration through executive orders, and there have been pushes to preempt state rules. States such as Colorado and California have passed their own AI laws covering areas like high-risk decisions and frontier-model transparency, some with delayed or contested effective dates. For a company operating across many states, it's a patchwork to track, much like state-by-state sports betting.

short: A database built to store embeddings and quickly find the items closest in meaning to a query.
explain: When a RAG system needs the five most relevant clauses out of ten thousand contracts, a vector database finds them in milliseconds. It's a standard piece of AI plumbing. Many traditional databases have added vector search, so it's increasingly a feature rather than a separate product.

short: When switching away from a vendor becomes so costly or difficult that you're effectively stuck with them.
explain: In AI, lock-in can come from prompts and integrations tuned to one model, data stored in a vendor's format, or contracts with minimum spending commitments. Because model leadership changes often, many companies design systems that can swap models easily. Ask any vendor how hard it would be to leave.

short: Digitally replacing or adding signage in a live broadcast, so different audiences see different sponsors on the same boards or surfaces.
explain: Computer vision tracks the field, boards and players so graphics can be inserted convincingly in real time. That lets rights holders sell the same physical inventory several times over, market by market. It depends on league and broadcaster approval and on tracking precise enough that the effect looks natural.
analogy: It turns one LED board into a separate sponsorship sale for every country watching.

short: AI that listens and talks: turning speech into text, text into natural-sounding speech, or holding a live spoken conversation.
explain: Newer models can handle audio directly, so spoken conversations feel quick and natural rather than robotic. That makes voice a realistic way to use AI in the car, on the go and in customer service. The same technology powers AI commentary and translation, and also voice-clone fraud.

short: A product that is mostly a user interface on top of someone else's AI model, with little proprietary technology of its own.
explain: Wrappers can be built fast, but they're vulnerable: the model provider can add the same feature, or a rival can copy it in weeks. Some so-called wrappers become strong businesses through distribution, deep workflow integration or proprietary data. In due diligence, ask what's unique besides the model.

short: A contract term where an AI vendor agrees not to store your prompts and outputs after returning a response.
explain: Enterprise AI deals often negotiate how long, if at all, the vendor keeps your data and whether it can be used for training. Zero data retention is the strictest version. It’s a key question for anything touching confidential, customer or regulated data.
